title: Fighting the Hypothetical: Why Law Firms Should Rethink the Billable Hour in the Generative AI Era
pub: 20 Washington Journal of Law, Technology & Arts 41 (2025)
author: Nancy B. Rapoport · Joseph R. Tiano Jr.

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Generative automation: Fluent work product still needs authority
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s account of probabilistic generation and emerging use for routine legal tasks, while treating usefulness and wider acceptance cautiously. However, it does not address the cluster’s central requirement that lawyers or judicial officers verify outputs and retain supervision and responsibility, so its overall position on the authoritative proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Big Law economics: Durable value exceeds firm size
st.an: The source accepts that Big Law’s future turns on structural adaptation rather than disappearance and materially extends the cluster by identifying origination-driven compensation and unsupported partner guarantees as specific threats to institutional stability. Its forecasts of smaller ownership groups, automation and outsourcing are explicitly qualified as predictions, consistent with the cluster’s caution against treating restructuring as inevitable incumbent replacement.
qs: But if the book of business vaporizes, or was never really there, and the partnership has guaranteed more in partner compensation than the partner actually brought in, that’s a Dewey & LeBeouf-style disaster waiting to happen.
Although Gary Munneke was optimistic about the time frame, he might still be right about the ultimate effect:                      The new law firm model will have a much smaller ownership base.

st.t: Billable hour: Faster matters need not reduce profits
st.an: The source accepts that GenAI pressures hourly economics without necessarily eliminating lawyers, demand or hourly fees, and materially develops the cluster’s practical middle position. It proposes classifying routine and bespoke work, using hybrid fixed/hourly pricing, and redesigning compensation, analytics, staffing and investment so firms can capture value beyond time while managing pricing risk.
qs: (“The value add comes from overlaying the flat fee approach with serious analytics on what things should cost to get the job done, and crisp project plans that show the client exactly what we will, and won’t, be doing for our flat fee, along with staffing plans that show who will be doing the work.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core concern that AI may erode traditional junior training and succession routes, while stressing that no settled solution exists. It materially extends the cluster by proposing solo practice serving underserved legal needs as a tentative alternative route for juniors to gain experience, alongside growing demand for AI-competent lawyers.

st.t: Firm tournament: Partnership extends rather than ends competition
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s systemic account of firm structure and partner incentives, then materially extends it to GenAI. It argues that compensation and prestige will shape technological adaptation, while alternative staffing may weaken associate leverage without necessarily reducing partner profits. Its claims are principally conceptual and predictive rather than measured outcomes.
qs: Consequently, as William Henderson observes, none of this statistical myopia is lost on law firm partners, who often valorize these metrics, rank them well above other values, and slip into the short-term thinking that those metrics represent .
Both of those factors are likely to play a major role in response to GenAI’s likely seismic effect on each factor.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source accepts that AI use cannot replace foundational hands-on legal work and materially extends the cluster by questioning how much traditional junior work is necessary and identifying the non-billable cost and institutional responsibility for replacement training.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central claim that GenAI threatens the pyramid’s coupled revenue, leverage and apprenticeship model, while predicting smaller junior cohorts rather than wholesale lawyer replacement. It materially extends the proposition with leader interviews, multiple possible successor staffing shapes, hybrid pricing and a proposed delivery model combining GenAI with third-party capacity, while acknowledging unresolved training and verification risks.
qs: When we say, “significant changes in how legal services are structured, delivered, and priced,” we mean that the law firm economic model will need to be wholly reengineered.

We don’t have the solution yet, but                    clearly, as AI takes over certain tasks, and as bankruptcy courts consider the use                    of AI in determining the reasonableness of fees under § 330, there will have to                    be a sea change in how new lawyers learn the ropes.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s copilot-and-verification framing by emphasizing professional risks and the need to check GenAI output. It materially extends the analysis by arguing that, where GenAI enables work to be completed quickly and accurately, avoidable inefficiency may itself raise fee-reasonableness concerns—making responsible efficiency an ethical consideration as well as a practical benefit.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central proposition that GenAI is a business-model problem and materially develops it through concrete proposals for redesigning staffing, pricing, task allocation, performance measurement and compensation. Its interview evidence also supports the cluster’s qualified conclusions that junior leverage may narrow and hybrid pricing may expand, while timing and the billable hour’s durability remain uncertain.
qs: When we say, “significant changes in how legal services are structured, delivered, and priced,” we mean that the law firm economic model will need to be wholly reengineered.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of selective, supervised task reconfiguration rather than wholesale lawyer replacement, including verification and apprenticeship risks. It materially extends that account with a concrete law-firm operating model linking AI adoption to leverage, staffing, billing analytics, hybrid pricing, proprietary tools and third-party delivery.
qs: We repeat our view that the current state of GenAI technology won’t replace lawyers (except for the lawyers who eschew GenAI entirely and have no other skills to bring to the table).

Tiano conclude their article by offering practical recommendations for law firms navigating this transition, including using billing data analytics to differentiate routine versus bespoke work, developing proprietary AI tools and processes, training lawyers to effectively leverage AI capabilities, and creating new billing models that better align with client value expectations.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source accepts task-level GenAI use rather than wholesale substitution and reinforces the need to preserve personalised, trust-based legal representation. It materially extends the cluster by identifying law-firm service-delivery resistance and existing profitability incentives as organisational barriers to converting technical capability into redesigned services, although its claimed cost advantage is qualitative and unquantified.
qs: Traditional law firms are often unreceptive to changing their service delivery methods.
The relationship is built on deep trust and confidentiality, with lawyers needing to understand not just the facts of a case, but also a client’s values, concerns, and desired outcomes.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source strongly accepts that GenAI will disrupt labour-based production and associate leverage more than eliminate lawyers or hourly billing. It materially extends the cluster by proposing a concrete operating model: use billing data to separate routine from bespoke work, combine AI with third-party providers for routine production, retain human review, and apply hybrid pricing to preserve premium lawyer judgment.
qs: We repeat our view that the current state of GenAI technology won’t replace lawyers (except for the lawyers who eschew GenAI entirely and have no other skills to bring to the table).
For routine work, a law firm would combine increased GenAI usage with the use of dedicated third-party partners who provide immediate access to an established infrastructure and talent pool.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core supervised-AI model: lawyers must verify outputs, exercise independent judgment, protect confidentiality, supervise use and bill honestly. It materially extends that position by arguing that safeguarded AI efficiency should drive value-oriented pricing, automation of routine work and shared client savings, rather than treating verification as eliminating AI’s commercial value.
qs: This client leverage should prompt successful firms to focus on high-value services that truly require human expertise while automating the “easy” things and passing savings on to clients.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that AI-driven value capture requires organisational and commercial redesign rather than task automation alone. It materially develops that proposition by linking billable-hour economics, staffing structures, external talent and technology, client pressure, in-house expansion, ALSP growth and multidisciplinary entrants, while acknowledging that change will be uneven and hourly billing resilient.
qs: When we say, “significant changes in how legal services are structured, delivered, and priced,” we mean that the law firm economic model will need to be wholly reengineered.

Potential catalysts for disruption include client pressure, an expansion of in-house legal departments, a growth in alternative legal service providers, and new market entrants combining legal tech, Big Four consulting, and traditional legal services.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, human-led deployment: GenAI automates routine tasks rather than replacing lawyers wholesale, while judgment and verification remain human responsibilities. It materially extends the cluster by proposing concrete redesign of law-firm staffing, workflow and pricing, including routine-versus-bespoke classification, hybrid fees and flexible delivery capacity, while acknowledging uncertain timing and labour effects.
qs: Still, lawyers should be deciding which tasks to delegate to GenAI, and those types of decisions should be nuanced.
When we say, “significant changes in how legal services are structured, delivered, and priced,” we mean that the law firm economic model will need to be wholly reengineered.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source accepts workflow disaggregation and the challenge to time-based production, then materially extends the proposition into a provider-side redesign of law-firm pricing, staffing, compensation and use of external specialists. Its case is more disruptive than the cluster’s cautious synthesis, but it qualifies adoption and timing and largely presents predicted rather than measured profitability effects.
qs: When we say, “significant changes in how legal services are structured, delivered, and priced,” we mean that the law firm economic model will need to be wholly reengineered.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central claim that GenAI pressures the billable-hour model, pyramid leverage and partner-development pipeline, while requiring firms to rethink service delivery rather than treat AI as a mere drafting tool. Its claims are prospective and qualified, especially regarding first-mover advantage and client uptake, consistent with the cluster’s caution that disruption remains unproven.
qs: Similarly, most law firms haven’t shown the nimbleness to compete effectively with alternative legal service providers and legal tech companies.49 The billable hour model and its economic dependence on human labor will impair a law firm’s ability to react quickly and aggressively, especially in the face of changing client expectations.

Not only will law firms that use GenAI responsibly have the ability to provide fast, good, and somewhat cheaper advice to their clients, the part of their overhead attributable to the old pyramid leverage model will likely decrease:219                    The larger implication for law firms will be about how they develop                   and select partners.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central proposition: automating junior production may shrink cohorts and deprive future lawyers of the hands-on experience needed to evaluate AI output. It likewise argues for redesigned training and baseline independent research and drafting before reliance on GenAI, while qualifying that competence does not require preserving seven or eight years of traditional junior work.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition that client-side pressure, including expanding in-house departments, will help translate AI efficiencies into changes in legal-service delivery, pricing and staffing. It specifically argues for automating routine work, passing savings to clients and shifting toward value-based economics, while acknowledging uneven, gradual disruption rather than established market-wide transformation.
qs: This client leverage should prompt successful firms to focus on high-value services that truly require human expertise while automating the “easy” things and passing savings on to clients.

Potential catalysts for disruption include client pressure, an expansion of in-house legal departments, a growth in alternative legal service providers, and new market entrants combining legal tech, Big Four consulting, and traditional legal services.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s core proposition that responsible GenAI will pressure billable-hour and associate-leverage economics while creating a staffing and partner-succession problem. It also supports differentiated pricing, continued reliance on premium human judgment and careful lawyer verification, while treating these effects mainly as interview-based forecasts rather than established market-wide outcomes.
qs: Not only will law firms that use GenAI responsibly have the ability to provide fast, good, and somewhat cheaper advice to their clients, the part of their overhead attributable to the old pyramid leverage model will likely decrease:219                    The larger implication for law firms will be about how they develop                   and select partners.

The current model of hiring a hundred                   associates, filtering them through many years, and then selecting 10                   partners from that group may be unsustainable in a world in which                   a law firm serves the role of prime contractor and engages in only                   more specialized legal analysis.

st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s core proposition that lawyers remain accountable for GenAI-assisted work and must understand the tools and verify outputs. It also documents AI-specific court certifications and bans while treating them as examples of contested judicial constraints, not as grounds for blanket prohibition.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core requirement that lawyers retain independent judgment and actively supervise GenAI rather than rely on it alone. Its contribution is limited to baseline ethical safeguards and does not materially develop the cluster’s broader claims about effective control, expertise development, or the adequacy of professional rules.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source accepts that GenAI can expand affordable legal information and basic services for underserved people, while limiting its case to task-specific assistance rather than autonomous legal judgment. It also recognizes verification, bias, confidentiality and unauthorized-practice risks and calls for continuing human oversight, though it does not substantially examine whether direct-to-consumer deployment shifts those risks onto users with limited verification capacity.
qs: The integration of GenAI is also opening up possibilities for addressing the longstanding issue of access to justice, with AI- powered tools making legal information and basic services more accessible to underserved populations.

GenAI can improve access to justice, making certain types of legal work more affordable to clients, though we also believe that humans need to continue to pay attention to all of the biases and flaws that any computer program may have.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source accepts GenAI’s potential to widen access to legal information and basic services while emphasizing that technical capability does not confer authorization to practice law. Its discussion of uncertain UPL boundaries and fabricated-case sanctions aligns with the cluster’s central concern that lower-cost assistance must retain protection, reliability and accountability.
qs: The integration of GenAI is also opening up possibilities for addressing the longstanding issue of access to justice, with AI- powered tools making legal information and basic services more accessible to underserved populations.
It already is doing so,109 and it has done so for a while.110         Whether the use of a self-service GenAI tool equates to the practice of law, though, is trickier than one would think.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core reliability proposition by describing fabrication as inherent to predictive text generation and citing the absence of any truth-checking mechanism. Its discussion of CoCounsel presents restricted sources and daily testing as safeguards, not proof that errors or the need for verification have been eliminated; however, it does not address verification costs or provide empirical error rates.
qs: One way of thinking about AI “hallucinations” is that the predictive “what should come next” model occasionally makes things up when answering the prompt.
(“A well-trained chatbot will produce humanlike text, but nothing about the process checks that the text is true, which is why we strongly doubt an LLM really understands what it says.”).

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The source directly supports restructuring rather than wholesale elimination: it predicts smaller junior cohorts, altered leverage and billing, and new AI-related skills while retaining lawyers. It also identifies the junior training pipeline as a central risk, though its claims are qualitative forecasts rather than measured employment effects.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source strongly aligns with the cluster’s proposition that GenAI requires operating-model redesign and can shift bargaining across providers. It argues that automation weakens the traditional staffing pyramid and hourly-billing economics, supports workflow- and matter-specific pricing, and identifies client pressure, in-house expansion, ALSP growth and new entrants as catalysts. Its uncertainty about timing, adoption risks and the persistence of hourly billing for unpredictable work matches the cluster’s qualified framing rather than opposing it.
qs: When we say, “significant changes in how legal services are structured, delivered, and priced,” we mean that the law firm economic model will need to be wholly reengineered.

Potential catalysts for disruption include client pressure, an expansion of in-house legal departments, a growth in alternative legal service providers, and new market entrants combining legal tech, Big Four consulting, and traditional legal services.

st.t: Partnership structure: AI tests governance beyond capital scarcity
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that technological change pressures the associate-heavy partnership model without proving that partnerships or their profits must disappear. It presents a prime-contractor/subcontractor alternative and explicitly treats the profitability outcome as uncertain, while offering conceptual rather than empirical support.
qs: This will require law firms to rethink their business model, but it is not clear what the impact will be on profits.
While partners traditionally made money by taking labor profit from their associates, they may be able to achieve the same result by marking up their subcontractors’ services.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source supports selective augmentation by distinguishing routine, non-judgment-intensive work where GenAI may improve speed and accuracy from tasks requiring genuine legal judgment, where it remains inadequate. It does not materially address verification, responsibility, junior development or staffing leverage.
qs: To recap, that’s considerably more accuracy in significantly less time.
Of course, we know that, for tasks that require real judgment, GenAI just doesn’t measure up, because it’s simply a multi-vector predictive model.

st.t: Supervisory accountability: Verification must test substantive support
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition that GenAI use remains subject to lawyers’ existing professional duties and requires human checking. It identifies competence, diligence, confidentiality and hallucination risks and reports ABA guidance to understand tools and verify outputs. Its treatment is less developed than the cluster: it does not explain source-level substantive verification, proportionate review or supervisory and institutional accountability.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition that GenAI will selectively automate routine legal tasks while lawyers retain judgment-intensive work, yet still reshape staffing and business models. It forecasts smaller junior cohorts, altered junior roles and hybrid pricing rather than wholesale lawyer replacement, while treating employment effects and training pathways as uncertain.
qs: Once a law firm identifies its easy-to-automate tasks, it can re-allocate that portion of the workstream to GenAI.69 Indeed, GenAI’s ability to do decent first cuts is commendable, if not remarkable.

kp.k: GenAI pressures hourly billing toward hybrid pricing
kp.d: The authors predict that GenAI will supply the external disruption that previous criticisms of hourly billing could not. They expect fixed prices for predictable, routine work and continued hourly or premium pricing for uncertain, judgment-intensive work, rather than the complete disappearance of hourly billing.
qs: In other words, the billable hour likely won’t die, but its useful life will be restricted to that work for which hourly billing actually makes sense.
Other aspects of work don’t lend themselves to pricing certainty, such as crucial depositions or protracted and intense deal negotiations; those types of work are better suited for hourly billing.

kp.k: Existing profitability reinforces resistance to change
kp.d: The authors attribute persistence of hourly billing to firm prosperity, inadequate collective client pressure, and the absence of a sufficiently powerful external catalyst. Drawing on the 2024 AmLaw 100 Report, they report that fifty-four firms generated at least $1 billion in 2023 revenue, Kirkland & Ellis exceeded $7.2 billion, and Wachtell Lipton’s annual profits per partner exceeded $8.3 million. They also identify change aversion, distrust of unproven technology, partnership governance and short-term compensation incentives as adoption barriers.
qs: Even though calls for the “death of the billable hour” have been made throughout the past decade,32 the calls have gone unanswered, partly because of this law firm prosperity, and the billable hour persists.
A near- term focus on imminent PPP results might lead a law firm to underinvest in GenAI technology or fail to train employees on the necessary new skills.

kp.k: Automation threatens the junior-heavy staffing pyramid
kp.d: The authors predict that automating first drafts, document review, due diligence, research and summarization will reduce demand for junior associates and weaken associate-to-partner leverage. They explore diamond, starfish and cylinder structures without claiming a single inevitable outcome: diamonds concentrate experienced mid-level lawyers, starfish organize specialized units around central management, and cylinders may characterize shrinking routine-work practices.
qs: Law firms will no longer need armies of junior lawyers, simultaneously removing some revenue and fixed costs from the economic model.
It’s fun to theorize, albeit impossible to predict, what the new model will look like in the age of artificial intelligence.
To be fair, different strata of firms will produce different shapes.

kp.k: Leadership interviews indicate change, not a uniform trajectory
kp.d: The article’s primary research consists of 30-minute interviews covering seven law firms and alternative legal services providers, involving chairs, managing partners, executive committee members and CEOs. Interviewees agreed that GenAI would change delivery, pricing and firm economics, but differed about timing and organizational outcomes. Several firms reported already reducing incoming associate classes; some reported technology expenditure exceeding real estate costs. These are qualitative interview reports, not market-wide measurements.
qs: We interviewed seven law firms and alternative legal services providers, asking such open-ended questions such as:
Several firms report that they are already reducing incoming associate class sizes.
The prevailing view suggests evolution rather than revolution, with different segments of the legal market likely to transform at different rates and in different ways.

kp.k: Lower revenues need not mean lower profitability
kp.d: The authors argue that automation can reduce delivery costs enough to improve profitability despite declining revenue. As a contrasting scenario, they report Toby Brown’s analysis of approximately $500,000 in timesheets from 10 large firms: drafting and reviewing accounted for 47% of sampled revenue; assumed reductions of 5% in partner hours and 20% in non-partner hours produced an estimated 13% revenue decline and 7% cut in profit margins. This is a modeled scenario, not observed post-adoption financial performance.
qs: Brown estimated a conservative 5% reduction in partner hours and a 20% reduction in non-partner hours.
That led to a 13% revenue decline and a 7% cut in profit margins.
Furthermore, with GenAI, it is possible for a law firm’s profitability to increase even though its revenue decreases.

kp.k: Lawyers’ work shifts toward oversight and differentiated judgment
kp.d: The authors expect smaller junior cohorts rather than wholesale lawyer replacement, potentially alongside more skilled paralegals. Junior lawyers and paraprofessionals would undertake GenAI oversight, project management and data analytics, while experienced lawyers supply judgment, creativity, interpersonal understanding and strategic advice. Their central model is supervised augmentation, although routine tasks may be substituted by technology.
qs: Instead, GenAI will automate lower-value, routine tasks that lawyers previously handled manually.
Junior associates and paraprofessionals will learn other quasi-legal skills, like GenAI oversight, legal project management, and legal data analytics.
GenAI can’t provide supervision, even though it might provide feedback.

kp.k: Reported performance evidence concerns specific automated tasks
kp.d: The authors cite the vendor LawGeex’s contract-assessment study, reported through a 2018 article: on a sample of five nondisclosure agreements, the system averaged 94% accuracy versus lawyers’ 85%, taking twenty-six seconds versus lawyers’ average ninety-two minutes. They use this task-specific evidence to support automation’s potential, while acknowledging that GenAI does not measure up on tasks requiring real judgment.
qs: with an average accuracy of 94% versus an average accuracy rate of 85% for the lawyers.
while lawyers took an average of ninety-two minutes to review five NDAs, the AI system needed only twenty-six seconds.
Of course, we know that, for tasks that require real judgment, GenAI just doesn’t measure up, because it’s simply a multi-vector predictive model.

kp.k: Clients may internalize work and demand demonstrable value
kp.d: The authors cite an August 2023 LexisNexis survey in which roughly 60% of corporate counsel across several major countries expected outside firms to use generative AI. They predict that in-house systems may remove demand for some outside work and envisage engagements beginning with client-supplied AI drafts. Firms would then need to demonstrate what their review and advice add, rather than recreate the draft.
qs: According to a survey by LexisNexis Legal & Professional, roughly 60% of corporate counsel across several major countries expect their outside law firms to use generative AI tools in their work.
On the other hand, nothing stops a law firm’s institutional clients from developing their own in-house GenAI systems, obviating the need for significant outside-counsel GenAI-generated work product.
Firms will have to figure out how to describe the value that they are, in fact, adding.

kp.k: Value pricing requires data, scoping and risk allocation
kp.d: The authors recommend using historical time-entry data to establish cost ranges, distinguish predictable from bespoke work, and support fixed fees, subscriptions, outcome-based fees and hybrid arrangements. They discuss sharing favorable outcomes and absorbing overruns, rather than leaving budgeting risk primarily with clients. They acknowledge that quantifying client value remains difficult and that clients may bargain for increasing shares of savings.
qs: Using time entry data to benchmark costs may not be perfect, but using some solid and verified data will always be better than guessing.

Outcome-based fees, fixed fees for predictable work, subscription-based models, and hybrid models align seamlessly with AI- powered platforms, because those types of models emphasize outcome, value, and results instead of inputs.

kp.k: Ethical use requires verification, confidentiality and reasonable fees
kp.d: The authors discuss competence, diligence, confidentiality, court representations, supervision and reasonable billing under the ABA Model Rules and Formal Opinion 512, issued July 29, 2024. They endorse understanding tools, checking outputs, exercising independent judgment and avoiding billing for hypothetical manual hours. They dispute the opinion’s suggestion that unchanged flat fees may become unreasonable when AI accelerates work, arguing that this privileges time inputs over delivered value and underrecognizes investment costs.
qs: That passage emphasizes the reasonable fee analysis only from a time “input” perspective, as opposed to a value output perspective (which is really what motivates a client to pay a lawyer).
It also ignores the reality that flat fees already incorporate the recovery of overhead charges, from keeping the lights on to paying for access to legal research databases.

kp.k: Licensure limits substitution but automation complicates legal boundaries
kp.d: The authors distinguish passing a bar examination from obtaining admission to practice. They discuss Model Rule 5.5, disputes involving Upsolve, and Lola v. Skadden’s treatment of judgment-free document classification in an overtime-pay case. These examples frame uncertainty over which automated activities constitute practicing law; they do not establish a general authorization for autonomous AI legal practice.
qs: But ChatGPT can’t get admitted to practice law, nor can other non-human programs.
The Second Circuit held, essentially, that, if a machine could do “it,” and the “it” required no legal judgment, then “it” wasn’t the practice of law.

kp.k: Inaccurate outputs can erase savings and require human judgment
kp.d: The authors warn that misleading prompts, fabricated output, compromised data and inadequately individualized advice can create expensive downstream problems. They emphasize that factual investigation, issue identification, contextual judgment and interpersonal counseling cannot simply be replaced by statistical output. Their treatment of Mata v. Avianca concerns sanctions for fabricated legal authorities, not a measured hallucination rate.
qs: And there are good prompts and bad prompts, the latter producing inaccurate results.
And when the software, or GenAI app, gets the advice wrong, the clean-up costs triggered by fixing the problem may eclipse the cost savings of the original “rote” work.
Even with good responses to good prompts, GenAI can’t take us all the way to being good counselors.

kp.k: Automating apprenticeship tasks risks weakening professional formation
kp.d: The authors fear that juniors who bypass drafting, research and document review may lack the skills needed to detect inadequate AI output. They report Judge Michelle Harner’s proposed issue-spotting training tool to supplement rather than replace mentoring, and David Wilkins’s view that some foundational junior work remains necessary without requiring seven or eight years of it. They urge law schools and firms to teach technological competence and redesign training as traditional entry-level work contracts.
qs: Skills build on themselves, and if the junior lawyers don’t have the underlying skills, they’ll have less upon which to build.
They may not know when the prompts have given them only part

kp.k: Access-to-justice gains remain conditional on competent support
kp.d: The article presents lower-cost AI-assisted services as a potential response to unmet legal need. It cites figures that 50% of middle-income households have at least one legal problem, only 20% seek legal assistance, and 26% do nothing. Reporting Damien Riehl’s proposal, the authors suggest juniors might gain experience serving previously priced-out clients, but worry about absent senior supervision and lower earnings. They favor carefully programmed bankruptcy assistance over unsupported self-help while recognizing exemption planning’s need for judgment.
qs: At the moment, studies show that 50% of middle- income households have at least one legal problem, but only 20% seek legal assistance, and 26% do nothing at all.
And we’re a bit nervous that the junior lawyers who hang out their own shingles might not have the guidance and perspective of their more senior colleagues

kp.k: Productized services illustrate opportunities, not guaranteed demand growth
kp.d: The authors invoke the Jevons effect as a possible mechanism through which lower costs increase demand and lawyer earnings. They cite Wilson Sonsini’s fixed-fee cloud-services sales-contract review product, developed with Dioptra by more than a dozen people over nine months using a 100-rule playbook. Wilson Sonsini reported 92% accuracy on rule matching and remedy application, with lawyer review before delivery. The stated commercial goal was taking work from competing firms; broader demand growth remains a possibility rather than an established result.
qs: They might even make more money, due to the Jevons effect.
A Wilson Sonsini lawyer reviews the work before sending it back to the client.
The goal for the product, Wang said, is to take work from other law firms.

kp.k: Competition may favor new delivery models and external providers
kp.d: Interviewees identify in-house expansion, ALSP growth and entrants combining legal technology, Big Four consulting and legal services as possible catalysts. Many predict greater disruption for mid-tier and regional firms than elite judgment-focused practices. The authors propose combining premium advisory work with GenAI and on-demand third-party personnel and infrastructure to reduce fixed costs. They also discuss proprietary tools, licensing and consulting as potential additional revenue sources, while reporting Susskind’s warning that commoditization can undermine product profits.
qs: Many predict that mid-tier and regional firms may face the greatest disruption, while elite firms are likely to maintain their position through specialized expertise and judgment- focused work.
In essence, this model would be a GenAI + “just in time” lawyering model.
Forward-thinking firms are exploring alternative revenue streams through technology licensing and consulting services.

kp.k: Courts may use AI as supplementary interpretive assistance
kp.d: The article discusses Judge Kevin Newsom’s concurrence in Snell v. United Specialty Insurance, where he explored ChatGPT and Google’s AI to examine the ordinary meaning of landscaping. His proposal was tentative and supplementary, not a recommendation that judges adopt generated answers as authoritative. The authors also envisage assistance locating trial evidence while cautioning against abandoning judicial authorship.
qs: Judges should not suddenly stop crafting their own opinions.
whether LLMs might provide additional datapoints to be used alongside dictionaries, canons, and syntactical context in the assessment of terms’ ordinary meaning.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Rapoport and Tiano predict that GenAI will automate routine legal work, weaken associate-based leverage, and push firms toward hybrid pricing and more technology-enabled, judgment-focused services.
pts.d: The authors argue that GenAI can produce first drafts, review documents, conduct routine research, and perform other recurring tasks much faster and more cheaply than humans. They predict that hourly billing will persist for uncertain, judgment-intensive work but increasingly give way to fixed fees for predictable work. They anticipate smaller junior associate classes, potentially greater use of skilled paralegals, and new responsibilities involving AI oversight, project management, and analytics. They explore diamond, starfish, cylinder, and other organizational forms without selecting a single inevitable replacement for the pyramid. They also predict opportunities for technology licensing, consulting, and combinations of GenAI with third-party legal delivery. Profitability could increase even if revenue falls, provided firms reduce delivery costs and capture value through new pricing. In-house AI capabilities could reduce demand for outside counsel whose contribution does not exceed what clients can obtain themselves. Early adopters may gain market share, while non-adapting firms risk displacement. The authors also identify risks: faulty output can create costly remedial work, and automation may deprive juniors of experience needed to recognize errors. They see potential for more affordable legal assistance and improved access to justice, while retaining human judgment and supervision.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article combines qualitative interviews, reported implementations, third-party studies and economic scenarios, professional experience, and legal authority; its market-wide forecasts are not presented as measured outcomes.
pts.d: The authors report 30-minute, open-ended interviews covering seven law firms and alternative legal service providers. Interviewees agreed that change was coming but differed about its shape and timing; several firms reported already reducing incoming associate classes. These interviews support reported leadership expectations rather than a quantified industry-wide employment forecast. The authors cite LawGeex's vendor study comparing NDA review: 94% AI accuracy versus 85% lawyer accuracy, and 26 seconds versus an average of 92 minutes for five NDAs. This is a task-specific AI comparison cited through earlier literature, not an evaluation of all contemporary GenAI legal work. They also cite a reported Wilson Sonsini–Dioptra fixed-fee contract-review product, with Wilson Sonsini reporting 92% accuracy against its playbook and a lawyer reviewing output before delivery. Fennemore's proprietary platform and Allen & Overy's adoption of Harvey are additional implementation examples. A reported Toby Brown scenario uses approximately $500,000 of time entries from ten large firms: drafting and reviewing represented 47% of sampled revenue; assumed reductions of 5% in partner hours and 20% in non-partner hours yielded a modeled 13% revenue decline and 7% cut in profit margins. These are assumptions and modeled effects, not observed AI-caused losses. A 2023 LexisNexis survey is cited for roughly 60% of corporate counsel across several countries expecting outside firms to use GenAI. The authors' training concerns draw substantially on professional experience and colleagues' observations. Their ethics and regulatory discussion draws on ABA Formal Opinion 512, Model Rules, Mata v. Avianca, Upsolve litigation, and Lola v. Skadden. Their Jevons-effect argument and first-mover predictions are economic reasoning and prospective interpretation rather than demonstrated aggregate demand effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The spring 2025 article describes adoption and some staffing changes as already occurring, but leaves the timing of broader restructuring uncertain and makes benefits conditional on responsible implementation and viable economics.
pts.d: The authors use near-term language such as 'soon' and 'in the future' rather than a firm industry-wide deadline. Their conclusion frames the transition as 'right now' and 'five years from now,' following interviewees Dan Reed and Aaron Crews of UnitedLex, but does not provide a quantified five-year forecast. Immediate recommendations include using billing data to separate routine from bespoke work. Interviewees characterize the likely trajectory as evolution rather than revolution, varying by market segment. The authors distinguish current task automation and augmentation from more speculative future capabilities associated with AGI. Their rejection of wholesale lawyer replacement is qualified by present capabilities, licensing requirements, and the need for judgment, empathy, creativity, and contextual reasoning. Fixed pricing is most suitable where scope and production costs are predictable; hourly pricing remains appropriate for uncertain negotiations and litigation tasks. Higher profits depend on cost reductions, effective pricing, investment, training, and sufficient demand. The proposed Jevons effect depends on lower costs increasing demand enough to offset reduced labor per task. AI output requires human verification, confidentiality safeguards, and appropriate supervision; the authors also acknowledge that error correction may outweigh initial savings and that competitive pressure could erode firms' capture of value.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects differ across firm tiers, seniority levels, buyer and provider roles, legal education, and underserved populations.
pts.d: BigLaw is the authors' principal lens, although they expect structural changes in MidLaw and SmallLaw too. Interviewees predict especially substantial disruption for mid-tier and regional firms, with elite firms better positioned to retain demand for specialized expertise and judgment. Equity partners face pressure on associate-generated revenue but possible gains through premium advice, reduced costs, and new revenue streams. Some interviewees foresee elite partner rates of $3,000–4,000 per hour; elsewhere the authors report interview predictions of up to $10,000 per hour for exceptionally targeted advice. These are predictions, not observed rates. Junior associates and routine-work providers face reduced hiring and hours, while experienced lawyers and skilled paralegals may become more valuable for reviewing AI output. The authors warn of diminished apprenticeship opportunities and recommend changes in law-school curricula and training. Corporate legal departments may obtain faster, cheaper work, negotiate more predictable pricing, or perform more work internally. ALSPs and entrants combining legal technology, Big Four consulting, and legal delivery may catalyze competitive change; software vendors such as Harvey are distinct from these service providers. Individuals and small organizations with unmet legal needs may benefit from lower-cost assistance. The authors discuss AI-enabled junior practitioners serving these populations, while expressing concern about inadequate senior supervision and lower earnings. Judges may benefit from assistance locating evidence and exploring language, without surrendering responsibility for opinions.
